title: The Annotated Transformer
hook: Want to truly get multi-head attention? Read the Transformer paper line by line — next to runnable PyTorch that implements every equation.
key_points: Reimplements 'Attention Is All You Need' as working PyTorch interleaved with the paper's text.
Multi-head attention runs several attention computations in parallel, each in its own subspace.
The heads' outputs are concatenated and mixed, letting the model attend to different patterns at once.
Walks through the full block: attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections, and normalization.
content_html: The Annotated Transformer, from Harvard NLP, takes the "Attention Is All You Need" paper and reimplements it line by line in runnable PyTorch, placed right next to the original text. It's one of the clearest ways to actually understand multi-head attention and the full Transformer block, because you can read each equation and immediately see the code that computes it.
extra_html:
How it works

A single attention operation looks at the data through one lens. Multi-head attention splits the model's representation into several smaller pieces and runs attention independently on each "head," so different heads can focus on different relationships — say, one tracking syntax and another tracking meaning. The heads' results are concatenated and projected back together. The annotated walkthrough builds this up from scratch, then assembles the surrounding pieces — positional encoding, feed-forward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization — into a complete encoder-decoder model you can run.

Why it matters

Reading equations in a paper is one thing; seeing them as executable code that you can step through and modify is another. This resource bridges that gap, which is why it became a go-to reference for people learning Transformers. If the original paper feels dense, working through the annotated version alongside it makes the architecture concrete and far easier to remember.

related.title: What Is Attention?
related.hook: Attention lets a model decide what to focus on: it scores how relevant each piece of input is to the current question, then blends them by those scores.
